summary:
Lunar Frontier is an educational, browser-based lunar colony management game developed by Team Problem Solvers for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, under the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge.
The project allows players to experience the challenges of establishing and managing a sustainable lunar settlement. Players begin by selecting one of 15 lunar sectors through an interactive 3D lunar atlas. They then establish a colony with an initial habitat and crew of seven, before managing resources such as water, food, energy, oxygen, metal and regolith.
Through a 2D management interface, players monitor daily resource production and consumption, construct facilities, conduct fieldwork and unlock additional sectors. Every decision influences the colony's ability to survive and expand.
The project combines interactive gameplay, simplified lunar settlement systems and research into NASA's open scientific resources to make space exploration and resource management more accessible, engaging and educational.
details:
Lunar Frontier is an interactive 3D STEM game designed to teach children aged 7–12 about the scientific and engineering challenges of establishing and maintaining a sustainable human settlement on the Moon.

Players begin by choosing a landing location and establishing a small lunar outpost with a basic habitat and seven crew members. They can explore the 3D Moon, which is divided into 15 selectable regions, and gradually unlock new areas as they collect resources and meet exploration requirements. Players can construct facilities such as solar arrays, hydroponics bays, ice extractors, oxygen recyclers and mining facilities.

The game requires players to manage six essential resources: water, food, energy, oxygen, metal and lunar regolith. They must balance resource production and consumption to keep their astronauts alive while developing their settlement. This encourages critical thinking, strategic planning, problem-solving and an understanding of sustainability.

The project was developed using Three.js, TypeScript, HTML, CSS, Vite and Vitest, with Visual Studio Code as the development environment and GitHub for source-code management. Player progress is saved locally in the browser, allowing them to continue their missions without needing an account.

The project's creativity comes from combining interactive 3D lunar exploration with a colony-management simulator. Instead of simply learning facts about space, players actively make engineering decisions and experience how resource limitations affect their settlement.

The main factors considered during development included scientific accuracy, accessibility for younger learners, ease of use, performance, visual appeal and educational value. The overall aim is to make space science more engaging, develop practical problem-solving skills and inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers and space explorers.
